title: Word order and 'to be'
description: Build simple sentences with the verb at the end, and know when Bengali needs a word for 'is' and when it does not.

guide.title: The verb comes last
guide.text:
The basic order of a Bengali sentence is subject - object - verb. English says 'I eat rice'; Bengali says 'I rice eat': আমি ভাত খাই।

Everything else - time, place, manner - goes between the subject and the verb, usually in the order time, then place: 'I today at-home rice will-eat'.

Because the verb ending already shows who is acting, the subject pronoun is often left out when it is obvious: ভাত খাই can mean 'I eat rice' on its own.

The order of the other words is fairly free and is used for emphasis, but while you are learning, keep the verb at the end and you will always be right.

guide.title: No word for 'is' when you say what something is
guide.text:
When a sentence says that A is B - a name, a profession, a description - present-tense Bengali uses no verb at all. The two parts are simply placed together.

এটা আমার বই - 'this my book' - This is my book.
উনি ডাক্তার - 'that-person doctor' - He/She is a doctor.
চা খুব গরম - 'tea very hot' - The tea is very hot.

This 'zero verb' only exists in the present. For the past you need ছিল (chhilo, 'was'), and the negative has its own word, নয় (noy, 'is not'); both are taught in later units.

guide.title: আছে: 'is' for where things are and what exists
guide.text:
When 'is' means 'is located' or 'there is', Bengali uses the verb আছে (aachhe).

বইটা টেবিলে আছে - The book is on the table.
এখানে একটা দোকান আছে - There is a shop here.

আছে takes the usual endings: আমি আছি (I am), তুমি আছ (you are, familiar), সে আছে (he/she/it is), আপনি আছেন (you are, polite), তিনি আছেন (he/she is, respected). That is why 'mother is at home' has আছেন: mothers are spoken of respectfully.

Compare: উনি ডাক্তার (He is a doctor - what he is: no verb) and উনি বাড়িতে আছেন (He is at home - where he is: আছেন).

The same verb gives 'how are you?': আপনি কেমন আছেন? - a temporary state, so আছেন is used.

examples.english: The book is on the table.

guide.title: No 'a', no 'the', no gender
guide.text:
Bengali has no articles and no grammatical gender. বই can be 'a book', 'the book' or 'books'; the context decides.

When you need to be specific, there are two tools. The ending -টা (-taa) on a noun makes it definite, like 'the': বইটা, 'the book'; ঘরটা, 'the room'. And একটা (ektaa, 'one') before a noun works like 'a': একটা বই, 'a book'.

Nouns do not change in the plural after a number or when the meaning is general, and adjectives never change at all: বড় ঘর is 'big room' or 'big rooms'.

phrases.note: ভাত is cooked rice; uncooked rice is চাল (chaal).
চেনা is to know a person or place by acquaintance; জানা is to know a fact.

phrases.english: The book is on the table.

phrases.note: The respectful ending -en is used when speaking about one's parents.
